newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Top U.S. diplomat calls Colombia's Samper corrupt.
newsitem.headline: Top U.S. diplomat calls Colombia's Samper corrupt.

text.p: A top U.S. diplomat said in an interview published on Monday that President Ernesto Samper was "an admirable politician" who is also unquestionably corrupt.

"There's no doubt in our minds about Samper's corruption," Robert Gelbard, former assistant U.S. secretary of state for international narcotics and law enforcement affairs, was quoted by Bogota's El Tiempo newspaper as saying.

Gelbard, who was recently appointed special envoy to Bosnia, has long argued that there was an overwhelming body of evidence to prove that Samper received millions of dollars in drug money to finance his presidential campaign.

Gelbard has been villified in Bogota because he led efforts to win Washington's "decertification" of Colombia's anti-drug efforts for the second consecutive year in February. The rare interview with him in El Tiempo ran under the banner headline: "The Hated Man Named Gelbard."
In a back-handed tribute to Samper, Gelbard said he was "an admirable politician who has shown great resilience" by surviving the drug corruption scandal that nearly forced him from office.

"He certainly is a survivor, there's no doubt about it," Gelbard said. He added that by clinging to power, Samper had done little good for anyone but himself, however, and said the embattled president had contributed to Colombia's growing isolation from the rest of the world.

"There's a sad air about Colombia," Gelbard said. "A majority of the people are honest. But a combination of corruption, drug trafficking, and the fact that a corrupt individual heads the government, have created a very unfortunate sense of isolation."

In the interview, Gelbard also criticised Interior Minister Horacio Serpa, a staunch Samper ally and outspoken critic of Washington who is expected to step down later this month to launch his own campaign for the presidency.

"I don't know him but I certainly don't admire him," Gelbard said of Serpa. "There's a suspicious air about him," he added, saying "a fat file" on the future presidential candidate had been opened at the State Department.
